steps.text: Bring the water to the boil in a medium pan and add the salt. Tip in the orzo and cook for about 9 minutes, stirring now and then so it does not stick, until tender with a little bite. Scoop out a few spoonfuls of the cooking water, then drain the orzo.

While the orzo cooks, pat the tofu very dry with kitchen paper and cut it into 2cm cubes. Slice the straw mushrooms, cut the ginger into thin matchsticks and slice the radishes thinly. Keep each one separate.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the tofu in a single layer and leave it alone for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden underneath. Turn the cubes and fry for another 3 to 4 minutes until crisp on most sides.

Add the mushrooms, ginger and radish to the pan with the garlic salt and black pepper. Keep the heat high and toss for 2 to 3 minutes, until the mushrooms are browned and the radish has just softened but still has some crunch.

Take the pan off the heat. Add the drained orzo, the butter and a splash of the saved cooking water. Toss until the butter melts and coats everything in a glossy sauce. Taste and add a pinch more garlic salt if needed.
Divide between two warm bowls and pile the sauerkraut on top of each. Serve straight away while the tofu is still crisp.

tips: Pressing the tofu under a plate with a weight on top for 10 minutes before cutting helps it crisp up.
Do not crowd the pan when frying the tofu. Use a second pan or fry in two batches if you need to.
Add the sauerkraut at the very end so it stays sharp and crunchy against the warm orzo.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan). Rub the lamb shoulder all over with 1 tbsp cooking oil, 1 tsp salt and the black pepper. Scatter the sliced fresh ginger in a small roasting tin and sit the lamb on top. Pour in 150ml water.

Cover the tin tightly with foil and roast for 3 hours, until the lamb is completely tender and pulls apart with a fork. Remove the foil for the final 30 minutes so the top browns and the juices reduce.
Rest the lamb for 15 minutes, then shred it with two forks, discarding any excess fat. Stir the shredded meat through the ginger-flavoured juices in the tin and keep warm under foil.

Rinse the sushi rice in several changes of cold water until it runs clear. Put it in a lidded pan with 260ml water and 1/2 tsp salt, bring to the boil, then cover, reduce to the lowest heat and cook for 12 minutes. Rest, covered, for 10 minutes off the heat.
Heat the remaining oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry the giant puffball slices for 2 to 3 minutes each side until golden and crisp at the edges. Season lightly with salt and set aside.
Wipe the pan, melt the butter over a high heat and add the enoki mushroom with the grated fresh ginger. Toss for 1 minute until just wilted. Take off the heat straight away.

Divide the warm rice between two bowls. Pile the shredded lamb on top with a spoonful of its juices, then add the puffball, enoki and pickled turnips. Scatter over the sesame seeds and finish each bowl with a spoonful of fromage frais.

tips: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan for a minute until fragrant, then tip them out at once so they do not burn.
If the juices in the tin look thin after shredding, spoon them into a small pan and boil briskly for a few minutes to concentrate them.
Keep the enoki cooking brief so it stays silky and does not turn rubbery.

steps.text: Take the steak out of the fridge 15 minutes before cooking. Pat it dry, slice it thinly across the grain into strips about 5mm thick, then season with the salt and black pepper.

Heat the grill to high. Split each croissant lengthways, leaving one side attached like a hinge. Open them out on a baking tray, cut side up, and spread the wasabi paste thinly over the bottom halves.

Melt the butter in a large frying pan over a high heat until it foams. Add the steak in a single layer, working in two batches if the pan is crowded, and fry for 1 to 2 minutes, turning once, until browned outside and just pink within.
Pour the water into the hot pan and scrape up the sticky browned bits for 20 seconds, then tip the juices over the steak. Take the pan off the heat.

Scatter the spinach over the wasabi on the bottom halves of the croissants, then pile on the steak and its juices. Top with the kimchi and sauerkraut, then cover generously with the grated Red Leicester.
Grill for 2 to 3 minutes, watching closely, until the cheese is melted and bubbling and the croissant edges are golden. Fold the top halves over the filling and press down gently.
Rest the melts for a minute, then serve each with a spoonful of cold potato salad on the side.

tips: Slice the steak thinly while it is cold from the fridge, which is easier, then let the slices come up to room temperature before frying.
Drain the kimchi and sauerkraut well so the croissant stays crisp rather than soggy.
Wasabi is fierce, so spread it thinly and taste a little before adding more.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Take the beef out of the fridge and pat it dry with kitchen paper so the rub will stick.
Bruise the lemongrass with the back of a knife, then chop it as finely as you can. Mix it in a small bowl with the rapadura, salt and black pepper.
Rub the cooking oil over the beef, then press the lemongrass mixture all over the surface so it is evenly coated.

Set the beef in a small roasting tin and pour the water around it. Roast for 15 minutes at 200C, then lower the oven to 160C (140C fan) and roast for a further 30 to 35 minutes, until the centre reads 55C for medium.
Lift the beef onto a board, cover loosely with foil and rest for at least 20 minutes. Meanwhile, peel the persimmon and slice it into thin slivers, and squeeze the sauerkraut dry.
Slice the rested beef as thinly as you can. Stir any juices from the board and tin into the beef slices so they stay moist.
Butter the insides of the bridge rolls, then brush the mint jelly over the butter.
Pile in the sliced beef, add a tangle of sauerkraut and tuck in the persimmon slivers. Press the rolls gently closed and cut in half if you like. Serve at once, or wrap tightly for a picnic.

tips: Slice the beef across the grain, as thinly as possible, for tender sandwiches.
Squeeze the sauerkraut well so it does not make the rolls soggy.
If packing for a picnic, keep the persimmon separate and add it just before eating.

steps.text: Pat the lemon sole fillets very dry with kitchen paper. Mix the plain flour with the grated fresh turmeric, the salt and plenty of black pepper on a plate. Press each fillet into the mixture so it is lightly and evenly coated, then shake off the excess.
Tear the butterhead lettuce into large pieces and divide between two bowls. Add the chopped kimchi to each, then set aside while you cook.

Warm the cooking oil in a small frying pan over a medium heat. Add the garlic flakes and fry for 20 to 30 seconds, stirring, until just pale gold. Lift them out straight away onto kitchen paper, as they darken quickly. Wipe the pan clean.
Toast the rye bread until crisp and deep golden. Set aside and keep warm.

Melt 20g of the butter in the pan over a medium-high heat until foaming. Lay in half the fillets and fry for 2 minutes without moving them, until the underside is golden and crunchy. Turn gently and cook for 1 minute more, until the flesh turns opaque and flakes easily. Move to a warm plate and repeat with the remaining fillets, adding a little more butter only if the pan is dry.
Turn the heat down and add the remaining butter and the water to the pan. Swirl for 30 seconds, scraping up the golden turmeric bits, until you have a loose, glossy buttery sauce.

Lay the fried fillets over the lettuce and kimchi. Spoon the buttery juices over the top, then scatter with the crushed peanuts, crisp garlic flakes and shavings of manchego. Serve at once with the toasted rye bread alongside for mopping up the juices.

tips: Dry fillets and a properly hot, foaming pan give the crunchiest crust, so resist moving the fish while it fries.
Grate the fresh turmeric finely and wear a glove if you like, as it stains fingers and boards bright yellow.
Lemon sole is delicate, so turn it with a flexible fish slice and cook it only until it flakes.

steps.text: Take the beef out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan). Pat the beef dry, rub with 1 tablespoon of cooking oil, then season well all over with salt and black pepper.

Put the potato chunks in a pan of cold water with a good pinch of salt. Bring to the boil and simmer for 8 minutes until the edges are just soft. Drain well and let them steam dry for 2 minutes, then shake the pan to roughen the edges.
Set the beef on a rack or in a roasting tin and roast at 220C for 15 minutes to colour the outside. Then lower the oven to 180C (160C fan).

Toss the potato in the remaining tablespoon of cooking oil and a pinch of salt, and spread in a separate tin. Dot with half of the butter. Roast alongside the beef, turning once, for about 40 minutes until golden and crisp.

Continue roasting the beef at 180C for 25 to 30 minutes more, until a thermometer in the centre reads 55 to 58C for medium. Lift it onto a board, cover loosely with foil and rest for 15 minutes. Keep the tin and its juices.
Warm the drained carrots in a small pan with the remaining butter, a pinch of salt and black pepper for 4 to 5 minutes until glossy and hot. Keep warm.

Make the gravy: pour the beef roasting juices into a pan, scraping up any sticky bits with a spoon. Add the vegetable curry and the water, and simmer gently for 5 minutes, stirring, until it is a pourable gravy. Squeeze in the juice of one orange, then taste and adjust with salt and black pepper. Add a splash more water if it is too thick.
Cut the second orange into neat segments, removing the peel and pith. Slice the rested beef thinly across the grain, pouring any juices from the board into the gravy.

Plate up: fan the beef slices on a warm platter, spoon over a little gravy, and top each slice with a few salmon roe. Add the roast potato and carrots, then the sauerkraut, orange segments and a spoonful of tartare sauce. Serve the rest of the gravy in a jug.

tips: Use a meat thermometer if you have one: topside is lean and turns dry quickly once past medium.
Slice the beef as thinly as you can and always across the grain for the most tender bite.
Add the salmon roe at the last moment so it stays plump and does not bleed into the gravy.

wiped clean and sliced about 5mm thick
topped and tailed, cut into 4cm lengths
a day-old one is easiest to tear

steps.text: Bring a small pan of salted water to the boil. Add the guar beans and cook until just tender but still with a bite. Drain, then spread them out on a plate to cool and steam dry.

Tear the croissant into rough shards about the size of a thumbnail. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over a medium heat, add the shards and fry, turning often, until golden and crisp. Tip onto kitchen paper and sprinkle with a pinch of salt. Wipe out the pan.

Season the turkey strips with salt and black pepper. Heat the cooking oil in the same pan over a medium-high heat. Add the turkey in a single layer, working in two batches if the pan is crowded, and fry until golden and cooked through with no pink left. Lift out onto a warm plate.

Add the sliced bay bolete and the crushed garlic cloves to the hot pan, with a little more oil if it looks dry. Fry, turning now and then, until the bolete is browned at the edges and the garlic is soft and golden.

Return the turkey to the pan along with the beans. Pour in the teriyaki sauce and the water, and bubble for a minute or two, stirring, until the sauce turns glossy and clings to everything. Remove the garlic cloves, or mash one into the glaze if you like a stronger flavour.
Tip everything into a wide bowl or tub and leave to cool to room temperature, stirring once or twice so the glaze coats evenly.

Fold the chopped celery leaf and the salami Milano ribbons through the cooled salad. Taste and adjust with black pepper. Scatter the croissant shards over the top just before eating so they stay crisp. If travelling, pack the shards in a separate lidded container and add them on the blanket.

tips: Slice the turkey thinly across the grain so it stays tender when eaten cold.
Pack the croissant shards separately and add them at the last minute to keep them crisp.
The salad tastes better after half an hour in the tub as the glaze soaks in, so it is ideal to make ahead.

steps.text: Peel the ginger with the edge of a teaspoon and grate it finely. Halve the takuan slices, or cut them into thin strips, and set aside. Have the boiling water ready in a jug.

Heat the groundnut oil in a large, deep frying pan or wide saucepan over a medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the lamb mince and chicken mince, break them up with a wooden spoon and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the juices have cooked off and the meat is nicely browned.
Turn the heat down to medium. Stir in the grated ginger, the nutmeg, the salt and the black pepper and cook for 1 minute until fragrant, scraping up any browned bits from the base of the pan.
Tip in the lentil pasta and pour over the boiling water. Stir well, making sure the pasta is submerged, and bring to a steady simmer.

Simmer uncovered for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often so the pasta does not catch, until it is just tender and the liquid has reduced to a thick, glossy gravy. If it looks dry before the pasta is cooked, add a splash more water.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with a little more salt and pepper. Divide between two warm bowls.
Crumble the onion bhajis roughly over each bowl so they keep some large crunchy pieces, then scatter over the takuan and serve straight away.

tips: Lentil pasta can turn mushy if overcooked, so start tasting a couple of minutes before the time is up.
Crumble the bhajis only at the last moment so they stay crisp against the hot gravy.
Takuan is salty and sharp, so taste before adding extra salt at the end.

Any pale ale you enjoy drinking

Peeled, grated fine just before serving

steps.text: Put the chicken carcass in a large pan with the water, sliced ginger and crushed garlic. Bring to a gentle simmer, skim off any foam, then simmer uncovered for 40 minutes until the broth smells rich and gingery.
Strain the broth into a clean pan, pressing the carcass gently, then discard the solids. Season lightly with salt and keep the broth hot on the lowest heat.
Toast the pecan halves in a dry frying pan over a medium heat for about 4 minutes, shaking often, until fragrant. Tip onto a board, chop roughly and set aside.
Melt half the butter in a wide heavy pan over a medium heat. Add the Vialone nano rice and stir for 2 minutes until the grains turn glossy and hot.

Pour in the pale ale and stir until it has almost all bubbled away, about 2 minutes. Start the oven or air fryer for the onion rings now, following the packet timings so they are ready when the rice is.

Add a ladleful of hot broth and stir until absorbed. Keep adding broth one ladle at a time, stirring often, for about 18 minutes. The rice should be tender with a little bite and loose enough to ripple when you shake the pan.
Cook the frozen onion rings until deep golden and crisp, following the packet, then leave them to rest on a rack or board for a minute.
Take the rice off the heat. Beat in the remaining butter and the grated Gruyère vigorously until glossy and creamy. Loosen with a splash more broth if needed, then season with salt and black pepper.
Spoon into two warm bowls. Grate a little horseradish over each, scatter with toasted pecans and crown with the crisp onion rings. Serve straight away.

tips: Add the broth gradually and keep stirring. The starch released from the Vialone nano rice is what makes the dish creamy.
Grate the horseradish at the last moment, as its heat fades quickly.
Add the onion rings to the bowls just before serving so they stay crisp.
